doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: What Longo learned from Dizzy and the Rhythmic Nature of Jazz DVDs
summary: Dizzy changed music organically, Longo played piano and trumpet with him even as he was dying, and everything learned is in his DVD series.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: What did you learn from Dizzy?

Oh man. How long a tape is that? The concept — Dizzy changed music organically. I don’t know if you remember Henry Pleasants. He was the classical music critic for the New York Times. He wrote a book back then called The Agony of Modern Music. The whole point of the book was the vital spirit that used to be in Beethoven and Mozart and those guys is no longer in classical music, it is now in jazz. And he specifically pointed out Dizzy and Charlie Parker. He said they represented the first organic change in music since Bach. He said they were able to discover a way of rushing at the wind and becoming airborne. So we have this thing in jazz about floating. And Dizzy ushered that thing in man. I can do it when I play but I don’t know what I’m doing. Dizzy knew. And so Dizzy — I spent an awful lot of time just he and I playing piano and trumpet because when he would be off he’d want to keep his chops up. So I’d go over and play with him. And when he was dying I would go over two days a week and play with him just for therapy. But he was still playing — what was that — Moody and I went over and said, © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

“Did you just hear that?” It didn’t affect his playing. He couldn’t hit a high F or something like that. But what I learned from Dizzy is, I have a four DVD series out called The Rhythmic Nature of Jazz that actually, in the order that I learned everything from Dizzy is the whole concept is on those four DVDs. And so they’re progressive. You have to learn this first, then the second DVD. But everything I learned from Dizzy is on those DVDs, in the order that I learned them. It’s very deep. Dizzy’s stuff was very, very deep, deeper than people realize.
